newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Yamani sells Swiss watchmaker Vacheron to Vendome.
newsitem.headline: Yamani sells Swiss watchmaker Vacheron to Vendome.

text.p: Former Saudi Oil Minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani Thursday sold Vacheron Constantin to Vendome, saying the future of the world's oldest top-quality watchmaker was best assured by a luxury group owner.

Neither Yamani nor Joseph Kanoui, chairman of Vendome Luxury Group, whose brands include Cartier, Piaget and Dunhill, would disclose the price paid after weeks of secret negotiations. But industry sources estimated Vendome paid between 100 million and 110 million Swiss francs ($77 million to $85 million) for what Yamani called "the jewel of Geneva."

Founded in Geneva in 1755, Vacheron has long made many of the world's most precise, finely crafted and expensive watches. In addition to new models, such as its Overseas range of sports watches, its older watches are avidly sought by watch lovers around the world.
Vendome is 70 percent owned by South African-controlled Richemont Securities AG. It was created three years ago from the combination of Richemont AG, Dunhill Holdings and Rothmans International.
Swiss experts lamented the loss of yet another independent watchmaker, following the acquisitions of Jaeger LeCoultre, Breguet and Baume & Mercier -- the latter by Vendome.

But Yamani, majority shareholder in the Geneva-based Vacheron Constantin since 1987, defended the sale. "This is definitely a great day for Vacheron Constantin," he said at a news conference where he clearly enjoyed the limelight.

"Today I am happy that all my objectives have been reached with the help of Vacheron management. The number of employees has doubled since 1987 and its shop, offices and factories have all been maintained in Geneva."
Vacheron made 11,091 luxury watches last year, priced from 8,000 Swiss francs ($6,100) up to four million francs ($3 million).
The private company, which does not release its figures, has posted 25 percent annual growth since 1987, according to Claude-Daniel Proellochs, its managing director.
Roughly 60 percent of its products are sold in Asia, including Japan, followed by 26 percent in Europe, 10 percent in the United States and 4 percent in the Middle East.

Industry sources expressed disappointment at the sale, noting that Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Girard Perregaux and Rolex were virtually the only completely independent luxury watchmakers. "The big names are disappearing one after another in the pocket of big groups," one said.
